## Different kinds of variables {style="font-size: 0.78em; line-height: 1.0;"}

<style>
.reveal section#different-kinds-of-variables .fragment p { margin: 0; }
.reveal section#different-kinds-of-variables .fragment ul { margin: 0.15em 0 0 0; }
.reveal section#different-kinds-of-variables .fragment + .fragment { margin-top: 15px; }
</style>

<script>

    var el = document.getElementById('different-kinds-of-variables');

::: {.fragment}
[Categorical variable]{.hl}: Responses are categories that **cannot be ranked** or ordered numerically. We assign a number to each category, just to make the categories easier to work with (e.g., in `R`). But the number does not have any *numeric* meaning. 

- **Examples?** [College major, religion, ethnicity, country of origin]{.fragment}
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Ordinal variable]{.hl}: Responses are categories that **can be ranked** on some kind of meaningful human-created numeric scale. The assigned number reflects the categories' rankings. However, we cannot be certain that the difference between each category is numerically equal.

- **Examples?** [Last completed education degree, strongly disagree -- strongly agree]{.fragment}
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Continuous variable]{.hl}: Responses are numbers that **can be ranked** and also have **equal unit differences** (a one-unit increase in the value of that variable indicates the same amount of change across all values of that variable). *More simply:* These are numbers as numbers. 

- **Examples?** [Years of education, income, country GDP]{.fragment}
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Binary variable]{.hl}: The variable has only two assigned values (typically 0 or 1). Often used to denote a yes/no condition. Typically, you name the variable whatever category gets a [1]{.hl}, and everything else is 0. 

- **Examples?** [**College graduate** (1=yes, 0=no)]{.fragment}, [**Republican** (1=Republican, 0=Anything else)]{.fragment}, [**Female** (1=Female, 0=Anything else)]{.fragment}
:::

---

## General rules and guidelines

:::{.incremental}
- [Continuous variables]{.hl} are the truest numbers and therefore best-suited for most of the statistical methods we use in this class.
- Most survey questions are [ordinal variables]{.hl}, but we will treat them as continuous variables.
- You can transform an existing variable into one with fewer categories:
  - *Continuous variable* --> *ordinal* or *categorical/binary* variable
  - *Ordinal variable* --> *categorical/binary* variable
  - **Note:** You lose some information/variation by "binning" your variable values into more general categories

- [If one of your variables is [categorical]{.hl}, you will need to transform it into a [binary categorical variable]{.hl} for this class.]{.hl2}
:::

- What type of variable is this? [[continuous variable]{.hl}]{.fragment}
:::

:::{.incremental}
- How would you turn this [continuous variable]{.hl} into an [ordinal variable]{.hl2}?
  - "Bin" them into three categories: autocracy, anocracy (semi-democracy), and democracy
  - *Note*: Researcher judgment in if/how to re-categorize the data.
- Why might you *want* to reduce a [continuous variable]{.hl} into an [ordinal variable]{.hl2}?

## Recall: Types of variables {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}


[Different types of variables...]{.hl2}


::: {.incremental}
- [Categorical variable]{.hl}: Numeric values represent categories that cannot be numerically ranked
- [Ordinal variable]{.hl}: Numeric values represent categories that can be numerically ranked; assigned numbers reflect an ordering.
- [Continuous variable]{.hl}: Numeric values represent numbers as such (numbers, counts, percentages, scales)
- [Binary variables]{.hl}: Variable with only two possible values (0,1), typically considered *categorical*
:::

. . .

[...require different approaches to quantify and visualize.]{.hl2}

---

. . .

For each of our variables (our IV and our DV), we want to understand and describe its:

. . .

[Dispersion:]{.hl2} the distribution of values of the variable

. . .

[Central Tendency:]{.hl} the typical values at the center of the variable's distribution

  - [Dispersion:]{.hl2} [25% rank (first quartile) and 75% rank (third quartile)]{.fragment}

## Describing **Continuous** Variables {style="font-size: 0.78em;"}

<div class="rank-stat-ribbon"><span class="gr2">Rank Statistics</span><span class="gr1">Statistical Moments</span></div>

::: {.incremental}
- [Statistical moments:]{.gr1} Statistical approach to describing a variable's central tendency and the distribution of values around it.
  - [Central Tendancy:]{.hl} **Mean:** The average value
    - Mathematically: the sum of all cases divided by the # of cases
:::

::: {style="display: flex; justify-content: center; gap: 0.6em;"}
::: {style="flex: 0 0 auto;"}
::: {.fragment style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; max-height: 30vh; font-size: 2.4em;"}
$$\bar{Y} = \dfrac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i}{n}$$
:::
:::

::: {style="flex: 0 0 auto; max-width: 62%;"}
::: {.incremental style="font-size: 1em;"}
- $\bar{Y}$ = mean (average) value (response) for variable $Y$
- $\sum$ = add everything that follows
- $i$ = each individual case of variable $Y$
- $n$ = number of observations (responses) in the dataset
- $Y_i$ = value of variable $Y$ for individual person $i$
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
![](10_variable_types_files/images/image18.png){style="max-height: 10vh; width: auto; display: block; margin: 0.15em auto;"}
:::

---

## Describing **Continuous** Variables {style="font-size: 0.78em;"}

<div class="rank-stat-ribbon"><span class="gr2">Rank Statistics</span><span class="gr1">Statistical Moments</span></div>

::: {.incremental}
- [Statistical moments:]{.gr1} Statistical approach to describing a variable's central tendency and the distribution of values around it.
  - [Central Tendancy:]{.hl} **Mean:** The average value
    - Mathematically: the sum of all cases divided by the # of cases
  - [Dispersion]{.hl2}:
    - **Variance:** The spread of the data around the mean
      - Mathematically: The sum of the squared differences between each value $Y$ and the mean value of $Y$, divided by n-1.
:::

::: {style="display: flex; justify-content: center; gap: 0.6em;"}
::: {style="flex: 0 0 auto;"}
::: {.fragment style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; max-height: 20vh; font-size: 1.9em;"}
$$\text{var}(Y) = \dfrac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}{n-1}$$
:::
:::

::: {style="flex: 0 0 auto; max-width: 62%;"}
::: {.fragment style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
![](10_variable_types_files/images/image21.png){style="max-height: 8vh; width: auto; display: block; margin: 0.2em auto;"}
:::
:::
:::

---

## Describing **Continuous** Variables {style="font-size: 0.78em;"}

<div class="rank-stat-ribbon"><span class="gr2">Rank Statistics</span><span class="gr1">Statistical Moments</span></div>

:::{.incremental}
- [Statistical moments:]{.gr1} Statistical approach to describing a variable's central tendency and the distribution of values around it.
  - [Central Tendancy:]{.hl} **Mean:** The average value; the sum of all cases divided by the # of cases
  - [Dispersion]{.hl2}
    - **Variance:** The spread of the data around the mean of $Y$
    - **Standard Deviation:** The average difference between each value of $Y$ and the mean of $Y$
:::

::: {style="display: flex; justify-content: center; gap: 0.6em;"}
::: {style="flex: 0 0 auto;"}
::: {.fragment style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; max-height: 25vh; font-size: 1.9em;"}
$$\text{S.D.} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}{n-1}}$$
:::

## Summary: Describing variables {.smaller}

::: {.fragment}
| | [Central Tendency]{.hl} | [Dispersion]{.hl2} |
|---|---|---|
| **Categorical variables** | **Mode** (Most frequently occurring value) <br> `table(data$variable)` | **Frequency** with which each category occurs <br> `table(data$variable)` |
| **Continuous variables:** [Rank statistics]{.gr2} | **Median** (50% rank) <br> `summary(data$variable)` | First (25% rank) & Third (75% rank) **quartiles** <br> `summary(data$variable)` |
| **Continuous variables:** [Statistical Moments]{.gr1} | **Mean** (average) <br> `mean(data$variable)` | Overall **variance** from the mean value <br> `var(data$variable)` <br> **Standard deviation** from the mean value <br>`sd(data$variable)` |
| **Ordinal variables** | ??? | ??? |
:::

---

## What to do with ordinal variables? {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

. . .

*Fundamentals* (3rd edition):

. . .

> When we move to the vast majority of statistical analyses, we must decide between treating each of our variables as though it is categorical or as though it is continuous... If we treat an ordinal variable as though it is categorical, we are acting as though we know less about the values of this variable than we really know. On the other hand, treating an ordinal variable as though it is a continuous variable means that we are assuming that it has equal unit differences. Either way, it is critical that we be **aware of our decisions.** We can always **repeat our analyses under a different assumption** and see how robust our conclusions are to our choices.

. . .

**In other words:** Think through which makes most sense in your case, try both and see if this shifts your results.

# Outliers and Missing Data

---

## Outliers {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

::: {.fragment}
[Outliers]{.hl} (continuous variables): Real cases in the dataset that are **extremely low** or **extremely high**, relative to the rest of the data.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- [Good to note your outliers.]{.hl} 
  - They might be worth examining more closely. 
  - They also might disproportionately **skew** your analysis and numeric understanding of the data.
  - Ex: Country GDP per capita (2024):
:::

::: {.fragment}
![](10_variable_types_files/images/image29.png){style="max-height: 30vh; width: auto; display: block; margin: 0.3em auto;"}

Source: @worldbank2024gdppc

## Missing data {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}


[Missing data]{.hl}: When the data for a specific observation/variable is unavailable.

:::{.incremental}
- For survey data: When a person does not know how to answer a question or decides not to answer the question.
- Often registered as extremely high numbers, low numbers, or negative numbers. But these numbers are **not real data** and will throw off your calculations!
:::

::: {style="display: flex; justify-content: center; gap: 1em;"}
::: {.fragment style="flex: 0 0 auto;"}

:::

![](10_variable_types_files/images/image9.png){style="max-height: 34vh; width: auto; display: block; margin: 0.3em auto;"}
:::

Polity regime-characteristics scores, 1800–2018 [@marshall2020polity]. Left: raw scores including -66/-77/-88 codes. Right: after dropping those codes.
:::

---

## Missing data

. . .

Two different ways that missing values are represented:

::: {.incremental}
1. **Weird or unreasonably high/low values** (e.g., -9)
   - `R` thinks these are numbers and will treat them just like any other!
   - Your measures of central tendency and dispersion will be inaccurate
2. **"NA" (not available)**
   - `R` understands that this is missing data (sort-of)
   - Your measures of central tendency and dispersion will break
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
(seen in: ANES, WVS, World Bank data)
:::

## Looking ahead: recoding & filtering your data {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

After the midterm, we will have a workshop to transform your variables. You'll be able to:

::: {.incremental}
- Create new objects for your IV and DV that drop missing values
  - `mutate()` &emsp; `filter()`
- Recode any categorical variables into a binary structure
  - `mutate()`
- Subset your data to only the countries/cases of interest
  - `filter()`
- Confirm that you have done so correctly
  - `table()` &emsp; `summary()`
- Analyze your descriptive statistics
  - `table()` &emsp; `summary()`
- Save a cleaned R script for your future use
:::

## 🔴 Try it: descriptive statistics — ordinal/continuous {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

`partyid` is a real 7-point party-identification variable (1 = Extremely Liberal … 7 = Extremely Conservative; negative values = refused/DK/inapplicable; 99 = "haven't thought much about it"):

```{r}
#| echo: true
table(anes$partyid)
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true
mode(anes$partyid)
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {style="padding: 0.4em 0.7em; border-left: 4px solid #c0392b; background: rgba(192,57,43,0.08); font-size: 0.85em;"}
⚠️ **Gotcha:** `mode()` does **not** compute the statistical mode — it reports R's internal storage type. For the most common category, use:
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| echo: true
names(which.max(table(anes$partyid)))
```
:::

## 🔴 Try it: descriptive statistics — ordinal {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

`income` is a real 28-category household-income bracket:

```{r}
#| echo: true
summary(anes$income)
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true
mean(anes$income)
sd(anes$income)
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {style="padding: 0.4em 0.7em; border-left: 4px solid #c0392b; background: rgba(192,57,43,0.08); font-size: 0.8em;"}
That mean looks too low for a 28-bracket scale — and that minimum is **negative**. Keep this on your radar; the "Missing data" section below explains exactly why.
:::
:::

## 🔴 Try it: spotting outliers {style="font-size: 0.78em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 2.3
#| out-width: "85%"

ggplot(anes, aes(x = income)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#107895", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "income (28 brackets)", y = "Respondents") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA)
  )
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
That spike at/below zero isn't low income — it's **refused / don't know / inapplicable** codes. Real outliers *and* missing-data codes can both show up as "extreme" values — you have to check which one you're looking at.
:::
:::

## Removing missing data

To get true numbers once you know your missing-data codes:

```r
summary(data$variable[data$variable > 0])
mean(data$variable[data$variable > 0])
var(data$variable[data$variable > 0])
sd(data$variable[data$variable > 0])
```

---

## 🔴 Try it: fixing missing-value codes {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

Before — contaminated by refused/DK/inapplicable codes:

```{r}
#| echo: true
summary(anes$income)
```

. . .

After — filtered to valid responses only:

```{r}
#| echo: true
summary(anes$income[anes$income > 0])
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true
mean(anes$income[anes$income > 0])
sd(anes$income[anes$income > 0])
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
Same real dataset, same command pattern from the slide above — the mean moved because the -9/-5/-1 codes are gone, not because the data changed.
:::
